title: Automated attack generation and defense-effectiveness metrics

opening.headline: There are limitations to manually crafted attack queries; how do we automatically generate attacks and determine what metrics to use for evaluating their results?
body: The number of attack queries a person can make in a day is at most several dozen. Attack expressions endlessly expand as combinations of vocabulary, language, encoding, and context, and must be rebuilt from scratch every time defenses are changed. Such checks are narrow in scope and become constrained by the imagination of the person conducting them.

In this class, we examine the principles of automated attack generation by modifying seed attacks to produce large volumes of adversarial inputs. We then explore what attack success rate and rejection rate measure, how their denominators differ, and how to distinguish the causes of changes.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain automatic attack generation and defense effectiveness indicators.
Success rate and rejection rate can be distinguished to interpret the metrics.

screens.title: Manual inspection has limited scope.
screens.lead: Read about where manual inspections performed by people encounter limitations.

paragraphs: The easiest way to check for defenses is for a person to directly create and launch attack queries. However, the number of queries a person can generate in a day is only in the tens. The same request can become entirely different input when vocabulary is changed, rewritten in another language, encoded differently, or when the surrounding context is altered. The variety of attack expressions exceeds what is feasible to manually generate.

A greater problem is that the outcome becomes trapped within the checker's imagination. Expressions the checker cannot conceive fail to reach the subject under review, and thus it becomes impossible to determine whether defenses can penetrate those expressions.

Additionally, every time defense is changed, the same inspection must be performed from the beginning. It is unrealistic to manually repeat inspections each time the prompt or model is modified. As a result, inspections tend to reduce to a single occurrence just before deployment.
Therefore, the question for this class is: how do we automatically generate attacks, and what metric should we use to measure defensive effectiveness?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: If checks are automatically run, the scope expands. Then, what should we examine to determine whether the automatically obtained results indicate improved defense?

screens.outro: First, let's recall the current inspection methodology.

screens.title: Check: Is automated auditing being used?
screens.lead: When you select a question, the instructor's thoughts are displayed. Please first think through the question on your own before entering an answer.

items.answer: Automation increases the volume of inputs processed at once. If not in use, defenses are typically assessed within the scope of manual inspection. If in use, the question of what metric to use becomes the next critical issue.

items.prompt: Is the same check automatically performed every time defense is changed?
items.answer: If rollback occurs, it is difficult to detect that the change re-enables the attack previously blocked. A consistent audit must occur for each defense change to enable comparison before and after the change.

items.prompt: If we summarize the inspection results with a single number, what would that number be?
items.answer: Usually, you only look at how many attacks were blocked. However, a single number indicates how many normal requests were blocked. This lesson covers the reason for reading indicators in pairs.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the principle of automatically generating attacks.

screens.title: The principle of automated attack generation
screens.lead: Select the right arrow to follow the flow where a few seed attacks expand into hundreds of evaluation inputs.

visual.alt: Diagram showing the flow of a seed attack expanding through transformation rules into numerous transformed inputs, and then being filtered again.
labels: Transformation rules (language, encoding, suffix string, expression rewrite)
Remove duplicates and noise, diversity analysis

steps.title: Creates an attack manually
steps.body: First, manually create dozens of seed attacks for each category. Seeds are crafted to mimic actual service inputs as closely as possible and are designed to elicit policy violations. The quality of automatically generated attacks is significantly influenced by the type of failure the seed represents.

steps.title: Define the axis of deformation
steps.body: We define the axis for how to modify the payload. As shown in OWASP's scenario, typical transformation techniques include multilingual content, encoding obfuscation, and appending seemingly meaningless suffix strings after the request. Additionally, transforming direct questions into indirect requests is also a common approach.

steps.title: Auto-increases
steps.body: Seed expressions can be varied using different models or transformation rules, leading to hundreds of variations. OpenAI documentation introduces prompt frameworks like Promptfoo as open-source tools that support workflows for generating adversarial test cases, observing target behavior, and using results for system improvement. Such a workflow can also be directly implemented.

steps.title: Execute and evaluate on the target
steps.body: Execute the crafted input on the target system and evaluate the output. Use automated methods such as safety classifiers or string matching for evaluation, but have humans verify ambiguous cases. Automated analysis expands the input scope, while human review handles ambiguous evaluations.

steps.title: Filters the quality of outputs
steps.body: Automatically generated content mixes duplication and noise. Sometimes, altered sentences are essentially equivalent to the same input or have lost their attack intent. Only inputs that demonstrate lexical and semantic diversity, originality, and clarity are evaluated and included in the benchmark set. A large number of examples does not necessarily result in a high-quality benchmark set.

screens.outro: Input is ready, so let's look at the indicator for reading the output.

screens.title: Defense effectiveness metric: attack success rate and rejection rate
screens.lead: When you hover over or select the terms displayed in the text, a description appears. Note that the input sets serving as denominators vary depending on the indicator.

data.text: When reading about defense effectiveness, the most frequently used metrics are Attack success rate and Rejection rate. Attack success rate represents the ratio of outputs that violate policies among attack inputs. Rejection rate indicates the ratio of requests that the system refuses to respond to, and its meaning can vary depending on the specific input set being considered. Within attack inputs, Rejection rate is close to the ratio of defenses successfully blocked, while within normal requests, Rejection rate indicates the level of Over-defense. Therefore, relying solely on metric names is insufficient, and Evaluation dataset interval serving as denominator must be included together. Success criteria are not vaguely stated as "safe," but instead are defined numerically—for example, as the ratio of requests classified as toxic out of 10,000 requests, such as Less than 0.1%.

terms.tip: The ratio of outputs that violate policies during adversarial inputs. A lower value indicates that defense is effective, but this metric alone does not reveal the damage caused under normal usage conditions.
The ratio of requests where the system refused to respond. The key to interpretation lies in understanding within which input set this occurs.
It is in a state of rejecting normal requests. This signal appears when the rejection rate within normal requests is high.

terms.term: Evaluation dataset interval serving as denominator
terms.tip: Indicates whether the input is an attack segment or a normal request segment. Even with the same rejection rate, it may mean either that defense was successful or that the service was disrupted, depending on the segment.

This is an example expression cited to illustrate how Claude documents measure against safety standards. It uses the ratio of instances out of ten thousand that are filtered by content for toxicity as the benchmark.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the indicator, let's look at how to distinguish the causes of change.

screens.title: Indicator Interpretation: Distinguishing the Causes of Change
screens.lead: Alternate between selecting the state before and after the change, and compare how the two indicators moved, and what that means.

states.label: Before change
states.body: Before enhancing defenses, attack success rate was high and rejection rate was low. Some attacks succeeded, and most normal requests were allowed to pass. These two figures at this stage serve as the baseline for subsequent comparisons. The baseline must be recorded alongside both the evaluation set version and the defense configuration version. For example, you might record the attack success rate at 8% and the normal request rejection rate at 2% in a single line. Otherwise, it would be impossible to determine whether subsequent numbers improved or deteriorated after changes. Additionally, intervals deemed ambiguous by the automated classifier are manually verified to reduce errors in the baseline itself.

states.label: After change
states.body: After strengthening the defense, the attack success rate decreased and the rejection rate increased. Looking only at the drop in attack success rate might suggest improvement. However, if the rejection rate increased even within the normal request range, it indicates that all requests were blocked rather than selectively mitigated. In such cases, it is necessary to break down the rejection rate by input type. An increase in rejection for attack inputs versus a rise in rejection for normal requests can have opposite implications. Metrics must be recorded alongside the evaluation set version to be meaningful for comparison. If the evaluation set has changed, it becomes impossible to determine whether changes in numbers are due to defense adjustments or data changes. Therefore, when comparing before-and-after scenarios, first verify that the evaluation set version remains the same.

screens.outro: Let's apply this interpretation with a real-world example.

screens.title: Explanation: In the case where the attack success rate has decreased but the rejection rate has increased.
screens.lead: The instructor walks through an example where two indicators cross in a step-by-step manner. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: Observation: Two indicators moved together.
steps.body: After strengthening the defense, we initiated automatic checks and found that the attack success rate decreased, while the overall rejection rate significantly increased. Within the team, there is now a consensus that the defense is working well.

steps.title: Question: Who is the one being rejected?
steps.body: The overall rejection rate is a number that combines attack inputs and normal requests. Simply knowing that this number has increased does not tell us which type of request was rejected. Therefore, the rejection rate is recalculated by type of input.

steps.title: Breakdown: Rejection of normal requests is most common
steps.body: Upon inspection, most of the increased rejections were actually legitimate requests. While the number of rejections from attack inputs had slightly increased, the number of rejections from normal requests had significantly risen. This fact would have been overlooked if the two categories had not been distinguished.

steps.title: Translation: It only broadly blocked.
steps.body: The conclusion is that defense has broadened rather than attacks being blocked. A significant portion of the reduced attack success rate is due to excessive defense that rejects even normal requests. The service has not become safer—it has simply become less convenient to use.

steps.title: Response: Narrow the rules
steps.body: Select a case of rejected normal requests and determine which rule blocked it, then narrow down the rule set. Re-run the evaluation set version to verify that the attack success rate is maintained while the rejection rate of normal requests has decreased.

screens.outro: Finally, we will look at how to record the results of automatic checks as documentation.

screens.title: Explanation: Recording automation results
screens.lead: The following is an example of execution records for a single automated check. Please verify, from the right-side explanation, what each line records and what issues arise if any line is missing.

notes.note: Include the execution number, evaluation set version, and defense configuration together. Without this information, we won't know under what conditions the numbers were generated, making it impossible to compare before and after changes.
This is the execution date. It is used to compare when the defense changed, and without it, it is difficult to link changes with results.
Indicators for the attack input range. Records attack success rate and rejection rate within the same range. Both numbers must be considered together for interpretation.
This is the rejection rate within the normal request range. Without this line, excessive defense appears absent, and the illusion of improved attack success rate is overlooked.
Identifier for representative failure cases. Attaching a few examples allows sharing with stakeholders, modifying them, and then reapplying the same case.

screens.title: Key points and reflection
screens.lead: Review the core of this course once again.

paragraphs: Automated attack generation transforms manually crafted seed attacks to significantly expand the input scope. However, the resulting outputs contain duplicates and noise, requiring analysis for diversity and quality, with ambiguous cases verified by humans. Automation does not replace humans but rather broadens the scope.

The success rate and rejection rate have different input sets as denominators. Rejections within attack inputs are close to the degree to which defenses have blocked them, while rejections within normal requests indicate over-defenses. Therefore, these metrics should be interpreted in pairs, separated by input type.

Records must include both the evaluation set version and the defense configuration version. Only then can the same inspection be rerun each time the defense is changed, allowing for comparison between before and after changes and enabling rollback when necessary. Manual inspections produce variable results at different times, making such comparisons difficult, whereas automated inspections can repeatedly apply the same evaluation method to identical inputs.

callout.label: Points to remember
callout.text: Simply hearing that the attack success rate has decreased may lead one to perceive it as an improvement. We do not conclude that an improvement has occurred until we verify the specific range in which the rejection rate has increased.

glossary.def: This is a method that modifies seed attacks to generate large volumes of adversarial inputs.
The ratio of outputs that violate policies during attack inputs.
The ratio of responses rejected during a request. Its meaning varies depending on the input set being measured.
It involves examining two indicators together with the input type to distinguish the cause of changes.

misconceptions.myth: A good defense is simply one that has a low attack success rate.
misconceptions.fact: If the rejection rate has increased as well, it could indicate over-defenses. The rejection rate from normal requests should also be checked.
The automated classifier assigns ambiguous cases for human verification. Automation expands the input scope, and humans handle ambiguous judgments.

misconceptions.myth: The more attacks generated, the better.
misconceptions.fact: When duplication and noise are mixed, even if cases are numerous, their usefulness diminishes. Diversity and quality must be analyzed and filtered.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Automated generation expands the scope, while human review takes on the ambiguous areas.
The attack success rate and rejection rate have different input sets as denominators.
The record includes both the evaluation set and the defense configuration version.

checks.q: Pair up indicators with their meanings.
left: Rejection rate within normal request flow
right: The defense success rate is nearly complete.
The ratio of outputs that violate policies during attack inputs
checks.explain: These three metrics have different input sets serving as denominators. The ratio of violating outputs among attack inputs is the attack success rate; the rejection of attack inputs demonstrates defense effectiveness, while the rejection of normal requests indicates over-defense.
checks.intro: Match the indicator name with its meaning. The clue is where the input dataset comes from. The result is not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: We accurately distinguished the denominators of the three indicators.
checks.incorrectFeedback: There is a mismatch. Please recheck the explanation regarding how the same rejection rate can mean different things depending on the input set.

checks.q: After defense strengthening, the attack success rate decreased and the rejection rate significantly increased. If most rejections were normal requests, what is the correct interpretation?
options: The ability to accurately identify attacks has been improved.
The evaluation set version is different, making the comparison itself impossible.
The ambiguous section deemed by the automatic classifier has disappeared.
Rather than an increase in attack blocking, it is about defense broadly covering more areas.
checks.explain: If normal requests are increasingly being rejected, it's not just blocking requests, but blocking everything. A response is needed to narrow rules by selecting specific cases of rejection.

wrong.0: If normal requests are being rejected more frequently, it indicates that the blocking scope has widened rather than the identification capability.
wrong.1: Version history is important, but the key insight in this case is the breakdown of rejection rates by input type.
wrong.2: The existence of ambiguous sections is unrelated to the interpretation of this situation.

checks.intro: When two indicators diverge, choose your interpretation. Results are not recorded.
checks.correctFeedback: Yes. If normal requests are being rejected more and more, it means defense is broadly blocking them.
checks.incorrectFeedback: This interpretation lacks sufficient basis. Please re-read the explanation to verify whether the rejection occurred from a specific input.
